bibliographic.title: An example of governance for AI in health services from Aotearoa New Zealand
bibliographic.authors: R. Whittaker, R. Dobson, C. K. Jin, R. Style, P. Jayathissa, K. Hiini, K. Ross, K. Kawamura, P. Muir, and the Waitematā AI Governance Group
bibliographic.citation_apa: Whittaker, R., Dobson, R., Jin, C. K., Style, R., Jayathissa, P., Hiini, K., Ross, K., Kawamura, K., Muir, P., & the Waitematā AI Governance Group. (2023). An example of governance for AI in health services from Aotearoa New Zealand. npj Digital Medicine, 6, 164. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-023-00882-z

methodology.sample_description: Te Whatu Ora Waitematā, a public health service responsible for approximately 650,000 people in Auckland, Aotearoa New Zealand; development and testing of governance processes with real-world AI proposals
methodology.technology_context: AI tools, algorithms, and machine learning models in clinical practice; no LLM or conversational system described in provided text

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article provides a detailed, empirically grounded account of establishing an AI governance body and framework in a regulated healthcare setting, with domains covering privacy, security, legal review, bias, transparency, and Māori health equity. It is highly relevant to governance and accountability in high-stakes health contexts but does not address LLMs, generative AI, conversational systems, chatbots, agents, RAG, or operational technical controls such as guardrails, tracing, or post-deployment monitoring at the level required for central evidence in a conversational LLM governance review.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Strong governance relevance may warrant elevation to foundational_contextual for regulated-domain governance synthesis, but scope mismatch on LLM and conversational AI requires human adjudication.

appraisal.notes: Clear practice-report objective and culturally grounded governance design; single-site organizational case limits generalizability; limitations discussion not evident in the provided excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: The account is internally coherent and grounded in real implementation, but it is a single health-service case report focused on broad AI/ML governance rather than conversational LLM systems; provided text offers limited detail on limitations and on post-implementation operational monitoring.

coding.subtheme: Culturally grounded governance framework with practical implementation

synthesis.main_claim: A comprehensive AI governance framework and governance body were established within a New Zealand public health service, integrating Te Tiriti-centered Māori perspectives, multi-domain review, and iterative testing with real-world AI proposals.
synthesis.contribution: Offers a concrete implementation example of an AI governance group, an eight-domain framework, and a proposal checklist spanning development to implementation, emphasizing transparency, equity, bias mitigation, and culturally specific governance in healthcare.
synthesis.limitations: Single organizational case; AI scope is general rather than LLM- or conversational-specific; extent of limitations reporting is unclear from provided text; sample size and outcomes of tested proposals are not specified in the excerpts.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence for institutional AI governance, regulated healthcare oversight, equity-centered accountability, and checklist-based proposal review; not suitable as central evidence for conversational LLM governance, guardrails, observability, or agentic/RAG controls.

evidence.claim: Article reports development and establishment of comprehensive AI governance in a health service
evidence.excerpt: Here we report on the development and establishment of comprehensive and effective governance over the development and implementation of AI tools within a health service in Aotearoa NZ.

evidence.claim: Framework tested with real-world proposals and iteratively refined
evidence.excerpt: The implementation of the framework in practice includes testing with real-world proposals and ongoing iteration and refinement of our processes.

evidence.claim: Study setting is a regulated public health service covering about 650,000 people
evidence.excerpt: Te Whatu Ora Waitematā, a public health service responsible for the health of approximately 650,000 people in a geographical district of Auckland, Aotearoa NZ

evidence.claim: AIGG uses one overarching question plus eight governance domains
evidence.excerpt: The newly established Artificial Intelligence Governance Group (AIGG) agreed on one initial over-arching question with further considerations in eight domains (Fig. 1).

evidence.claim: Governance checklist spans workflow from development to implementation and includes machine learning expertise
evidence.excerpt: adapting all of the above into a checklist for use by the AIGG when considering new proposals for access to data or clinicians at any stage of the AI development workflow from development to implementation

evidence.claim: Checklist representation includes privacy, security, legal, Māori health, and machine learning expertise
evidence.excerpt: consumers, clinical governance, data and digital governance, privacy and security, legal, Māori health, Pacific Island health, research, analytics, innovation and improvement (supporting implementation), and external expertise in AI and machine learning.

evidence.claim: Transparency is required to build clinician trust and support safe decisions
evidence.excerpt: A high level of transparency is required to build trust amongst clinicians ensuring any decisions based upon model outputs are well understood, safe and accurate.

evidence.claim: Governance addresses equity, fairness, and bias in data or models
evidence.excerpt: Equity and fairness particularly focus on the likelihood of any bias or discrimination issues that may exist in the data collected or are unintentionally introduced by the model.

evidence.claim: Māori perspectives support Te Tiriti-based accountability and acceptability
evidence.excerpt: The inclusion of Māori perspectives in the AIGG also encourages Te Tiriti based arrangements, ensuring acceptability and accountability to Māori with a commitment to equitable benefits through a sustained focus on mana (mutual respect).

evidence.claim: No conversational AI or LLM-specific technology is described in the provided text
evidence.excerpt: external expertise in AI and machine learning.
